# 2026-11-22: What a part's history can say without limit {.unnumbered}

::: {.callout-note appearance="minimal" icon="false"}
**Status:** exploratory · **Thread:** T11 · **Checked by:** `tests/test_scale.py`, `tests/test_bench_t11.py`
:::

**Question.** The [note on payload mass](2026-11-22-mass-and-resolution.qmd) found that a
body's history says more and more about its masses and dampings the faster the motion it
resolves, while what it says about the ground's stiffness settles. The energy metric has no
time scale of its own; the uniqueness theorem demands that (requirement U3 of
@thm-unique). So which properties of the environment have a finite answer per second
without an outside scale, and which need a stated band?

**Short answer.** One number decides. At high frequency a part's thermal motion has the
spectrum $c/\omega^4$, with
$$
c=2\sigma_T^2\,p^\top H^{-1}DH^{-1}p ,
$$
set by the inertia and the damping that the part feels directly. If a property leaves $c$
unchanged, the part's history holds a finite amount about it per second, however finely
the motion is resolved. If it changes $c$, the information grows by
$(\partial_\theta\log c)^2$ per second for every extra hertz.

For a body of point masses joined by elements, $c$ involves only the part's own mass and
the dampers attached to it. So a part learns without limit only about what it touches.
About everything else (masses elsewhere, dampers elsewhere, and every stiffness, the
ground's included) its history holds a finite amount per second. On the SEA the rotor
holds a finite 31.2 per second about the link's mass, while the link itself gains 4 per
second per hertz.

This keeps the history view of the book: what a part holds is what its whole trajectory
holds. The price of that view is a stated band for the few properties a part touches.

## Setting

A linear body with symmetric $H$, $K$, $D$ and the Langevin body's white thermal force
(@sec-langevin). A part is one coordinate $y=p^\top q$, observed over a long window with
its motion resolved up to a band of $B$ hertz. The unknown $\theta$ is the log of one
property: a mass, a damping or a stiffness. The checks use the SEA at $k_s=10^3$ N m/rad,
with the link and the rotor as parts.

## Results

::: {#thm-leading name="The leading coefficient decides"}
Let $c(\theta)=p^\top H^{-1}DH^{-1}p>0$. As the band $B$ grows, the information rate about
$\theta$ held by the part's history behaves as
$$
\dot I(B)=\big(\partial_\theta\log c\big)^2\,B+O(1).
$$
In particular it stays bounded exactly when $c$ does not depend on $\theta$.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
*Step 1: the rate from the spectrum.* For a long window, a stationary Gaussian signal with
spectrum $S_\theta(\omega)$ carries Fisher information about $\theta$ at the rate
$\frac1{4\pi}\int_{|\omega|<2\pi B}(\partial_\theta\log S_\theta)^2\,d\omega$ per second (Whittle's
formula [@whittle1953analysis]).

*Step 2: the spectrum at high frequency.* The part's spectrum is
$S=2\sigma_T^2\,p^\top YDY^*p$ with $Y=(K-\omega^2H+i\omega D)^{-1}$. Expanding for large
$\omega$,
$$
Y=-\frac{H^{-1}}{\omega^2}-\frac{i\,H^{-1}DH^{-1}}{\omega^3}+O(\omega^{-4}).
$$
Inserting this, the two cross terms of order $\omega^{-5}$ are equal and opposite and
cancel, so $S=\frac{2\sigma_T^2}{\omega^4}\big(c+O(\omega^{-2})\big)$.

*Step 3: the log-derivative.* Since $c>0$,
$\log S=\log(2\sigma_T^2)-4\log\omega+\log c+O(\omega^{-2})$, and
$\partial_\theta\log S=\partial_\theta\log c+O(\omega^{-2})$, because every term is a rational
function of $\omega$ that depends smoothly on $\theta$.

*Step 4: the integral.* If $\partial_\theta\log c\ne0$, the integrand tends to
$(\partial_\theta\log c)^2$, and the integral over $|\omega|<2\pi B$ is
$(\partial_\theta\log c)^2B+O(1)$. If $\partial_\theta\log c=0$, the integrand is $O(\omega^{-4})$
and the integral converges.

*What is not proved here.* The error terms of Whittle's formula. The case $c=0$, a part
with no damping reaching it at leading order, where the next term of the expansion decides.
:::

Over a finite window the same dichotomy has a classical form. Two Gaussian processes with
rational spectra are, on any finite interval, either impossible to tell apart with
certainty or certain to be told apart, according to whether their spectra agree at high
frequency [@ibragimov1978gaussian]. Here that means a property that changes $c$ is
determined exactly by any stretch of a perfectly resolved history. The book does not rely
on this result; it is the finite-window counterpart of @thm-leading.

::: {#cor-touch name="A part learns without limit only about what it touches"}
Let the body be point masses joined by spring-damper elements, so that $H$ is diagonal,
and let the part be node $k$ with mass $m_k$. Then
$$
c=\frac{D_{kk}}{m_k^2},\qquad D_{kk}=\sum_{j\ \text{attached to}\ k}b_j ,
$$
the sum running over the dampers attached to node $k$, the ground damper included if $k$
touches the ground. The part's information grows with the band

- about its own mass, by 4 per second per hertz;
- about a damper $b_j$ attached to it, by $(b_j/D_{kk})^2$ per second per hertz;

and stays finite about every other mass, every damper not attached to it, and every
stiffness.
:::

::: {.proof}
With $H$ diagonal, $p^\top H^{-1}DH^{-1}p=D_{kk}/m_k^2$ for $p=e_k$. An element between
nodes $i$ and $j$ adds $b$ to $D_{ii}$ and $D_{jj}$ and nothing else on the diagonal, so
$D_{kk}$ is the sum of the dampers attached to $k$. Then $\partial\log c/\partial\log m_k=-2$,
$\partial\log c/\partial\log b_j=b_j/D_{kk}$ for an attached damper, and 0 for any other
property. @thm-leading gives the rates.
:::

The SEA, in joint coordinates, fits this form: $H=\diag(m_lr^2,I_{\rm rot})$, the link
carries the ground damper $b_cr^2=6$ and the series damper $b_s=0.63$, and the rotor
carries only $b_s$. The corollary predicts:

- the link gains 4 per hertz about its mass, $(6/6.63)^2=0.82$ about the ground damping
    and $(0.63/6.63)^2=0.009$ about the series damper;
- the rotor gains 1 per hertz about the series damper;
- everything else is finite: the rotor about the link's mass and the ground damping, and
    both parts about both stiffnesses.

The rigid leg has one coordinate whose inertia combines link and rotor, so its own mass is
only partly the link's: $\partial\log c/\partial\log m_l=-2\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon=0.75$,
and the growth $(2\varepsilon)^2=2.25$ of the mass note.

## Numbers

| property | part | 800 Hz | 1,600 Hz | 3,200 Hz | growth per Hz | predicted |
|:--|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| link mass | link | 3,551.6 | 6,792.1 | 13,212.2 | 4.013 | 4 |
| link mass | rotor | 31.2 | 31.2 | 31.2 | 0 | 0 |
| ground damping | link | 553.4 | 1,205.1 | 2,513.0 | 0.817 | 0.818 |
| ground damping | rotor | 4.5 | 4.5 | 4.5 | 0 | 0 |
| series damping | link | 11.3 | 18.6 | 33.1 | 0.009 | 0.009 |
| series damping | rotor | 712.5 | 1,511.9 | 3,111.7 | 1.000 | 1 |
| ground stiffness | link | 635.1 | 635.3 | 635.3 | 0 | 0 |
| ground stiffness | rotor | 43.2 | 43.2 | 43.2 | 0 | 0 |
| series stiffness | link | 96.9 | 96.9 | 96.9 | 0 | 0 |
| series stiffness | rotor | 649.7 | 649.7 | 649.7 | 0 | 0 |

: Fisher information per second about the log of each property, held by the history of one part of the SEA ($k_s=10^3$), with its motion resolved up to each band, sampled at 64 kHz (`check_criterion`). The growth is measured between 1,600 and 3,200 Hz; the prediction is $(\partial_\theta\log c)^2$. When the series stiffness changes, $b_s$ is held fixed. {#tbl-criterion}

All ten predictions hold: the growth matches $(\partial_\theta\log c)^2$ to within 0.013 per
hertz, and every property predicted to be finite changes by at most 0.2 per second from
800 to 3,200 Hz.

## What this changes

The history view stays. What a part holds about its environment is what its whole
trajectory holds, which is what computation over time will need. @thm-leading says when
that is finite without an outside scale: whenever the property does not change the part's
own inertia and damping. A part's history holds a finite amount per second about the
ground's stiffness, about masses elsewhere in the body and about dampers it does not
touch. For the few properties a part touches, its own mass and its own dampers, the answer
depends on the band, and the book states one. For the whole body, which touches all its
masses and dampers, every mass and damping question needs a band.

This refines the proposal of the mass note: a band is needed only where @cor-touch says the
part touches the property.

## Limits of this note

- Linear bodies with the white-noise Langevin body. The mass note shows that a bath with
    finite memory leaves the growth unchanged; the criterion for such baths would use the
    bath's own high-frequency spectrum.
- One-coordinate parts. For several coordinates the same argument gives the growth
    $\operatorname{tr}\big[(C^{-1}\partial_\theta C)^2\big]$ per hertz, with $C$ the leading
    matrix coefficient; this is not checked here.
- The case $c=0$ is not treated.

## Next steps

- Check the several-coordinate form, and a chain, where a node far from a payload should
    hold a finite amount about it.
- Use the criterion in the nonlinear thread (T7), where the high-frequency behaviour may
    differ.

## Checks of 2026-11-25

The roadmap asked for four checks before this note and the
[mass note](2026-11-22-mass-and-resolution.qmd) go into a chapter (thread T11). Three are
done here; the fourth is a question of definition, recorded in the roadmap. Code:
`mibook.bench.t11`; tests: `tests/test_bench_t11.py`.

**1. The formula against a source read in full.** Whittle's formula is confirmed in the
form used by system identification. @ljung1999system [Eqs. 13.24–13.26, pp. 416–417]
gives the information per sample about a parameter of a sampled model $y=Gu+He$ as an
input-driven term plus a noise term, $M_e=\frac{\lambda_0^2}{2\pi\kappa_0}\int H'_\theta
H'^{*}_\theta/\Phi_v\,d\omega$. For Gaussian innovations whose variance does not depend on the
parameter, and a noise filter $H$ that is monic, stable and stably invertible, $M_e$ equals
the per-sample Whittle rate: the real and imaginary parts of $\partial\log H$ then carry equal
energy over the band, which turns Ljung's integral of $|\partial\log H|^2$ into Whittle's
integral of $(\partial\log\Phi_v)^2/4$. When the innovation variance does depend on the
parameter, Whittle's formula already includes it; Ljung's split needs an extra term. The
original sources of @whittle1953analysis and @ibragimov1978gaussian remain unread.

**2. Finite windows, without Whittle's formula.** The information over a finite window is
now computed exactly in time linear in the window (`linear.window_fisher`): the relative
entropy between the part's motion at $\theta\pm h$ comes from two Kalman filters and the
joint covariance of one body's state and the other body's estimate. It agrees with the
book's stacked computation (71.213 against 71.213; 3.3453 against 3.3456). On the SEA
($k_s=10^3$) the slope between windows of 0.1 and 0.4 s agrees with the spectral rate to
four digits for every case, for example 8,398.1 against 8,398.1 per second about the link's
mass at the link and 31.13 against 31.15 at the rotor. As the sampling rate doubles from 2 to
16 kHz, the exact finite-window rate about the link's mass at the link grows by 4.00 per
hertz, while the rotor's (31.1) and the ground stiffness's (635.5 and 43.2) stay put.

One caution came out of this check. For a lightly damped body, the spectral rate needs a
very fine frequency grid: on a chain whose slowest mode decays in 7 s, a grid of 0.25 Hz
gave 559 where the exact value is 522, and only a grid of 0.008 Hz recovered it. The
finite-window computation has no grid and is the safer check.

**3. Parts with several coordinates.** @thm-leading extends to a part read through several
coordinates, with the matrix $c=PH^{-1}DH^{-1}P^\top$ for a selector $P$ of the part's
positions.

::: {#prp-leading-matrix name="The leading coefficient for several coordinates"}
For a part with position selector $P$ and $c=PH^{-1}DH^{-1}P^\top\succ0$, the information rate
about $\theta$ grows with the band as
$\dot I(B)=\operatorname{tr}\big[(c^{-1}\partial_\theta c)^2\big]\,B+O(1)$.
:::

::: {.proof name="Proof sketch"}
Steps 2 to 4 of the proof of @thm-leading carry over with matrices. The part's spectrum is
$S=\frac{2\sigma_T^2}{\omega^4}\big(c+O(\omega^{-2})\big)$, so
$S^{-1}\partial_\theta S=c^{-1}\partial_\theta c+O(\omega^{-2})$. Whittle's rate for a vector
signal is $\frac1{4\pi}\int\operatorname{tr}[(S^{-1}\partial_\theta S)^2]\,d\omega$, whose integrand
tends to $\operatorname{tr}[(c^{-1}\partial_\theta c)^2]$; integrating over $|\omega|<2\pi B$ gives
$B\operatorname{tr}[(c^{-1}\partial_\theta c)^2]+O(1)$. For one coordinate this is
@thm-leading. The error terms are not proved, as before.
:::

On a three-mass grounded chain the exact finite-window rates agree with this to three
decimals:

| part (nodes) | mass 0 | mass 1 | mass 2 |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| node 1 | finite (0.4 per s) | 4.000 (predicted 4) | finite (16.9 per s) |
| nodes 1 and 2 | finite (4.6 per s) | 7.332 (7.333) | 7.333 (7.333) |
| all three | 5.498 (5.500) | 11.329 (11.333) | 9.832 (9.833) |

Growth per hertz, from sampling rates of 1 to 8 kHz. So a part learns without limit about
exactly the masses it contains, and the rate per hertz depends on how those masses share the
dampers between them.

**4. Whether a part's own mass is "environment".** This is a question of definition, not of
calculation, and is left to the reviewer (see the roadmap).
